March 2, 2026 
Submitted Electronically 
 
Administrator Mehmet Oz 
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services 
7500 Security Boulevard 
Baltimore, MD 21244-1850 
 
Re: CMS-9882-P Transparency in Coverage Proposed Rule 
 
We applaud the Departmentsâ€™ progress in making the Transparency in Coverage (TIC) files more 
usable.  We are particularly pleased to see the proposal for introduction of network-level data 
files. This change will more closely match the TIC file data elements to the contract and price 
schedule entities that the data is intended to represent, resulting in smaller files and greatly 
improved data quality. 
Our comments address problems with the use of network names and present 
recommendations for the development of a standardized network identifier via an industry 
working group. 
 
Problems with Network Names 
We have serious concerns around the use of a network name rather than a formal network 
identifier as a means to identify the network within TIC files.  Ambiguous network names 
degrade the quality and utility of the data reported in TIC files, for a number of reasons: 
â€¢ Ambiguity around the identity of the network - Carriers sometimes use different names 
to represent a single network, or the same or similar names to reference different 
networks. The name itself is not a strong enough identifier. 
 
â€¢ Ambiguous network names will limit the ability of data users to accurately link plan 
designs to network rates. Price data is most actionable for consumers, employers, and 
others when it can be accurately linked to a specific health plan design with its 
 
 
  
deductibles, copays, out of pocket limits, and other rules regarding coverage such as 
prior authorization requirements and medical necessity criteria.  
 
â€¢ Inability to link data to provider directories - Directories are filtered by plan, by network, 
or by â€˜generalizedâ€™ network. It is currently difficult for consumers to know which filters 
to choose with many similar network names and without an identifier. Apps relying on 
interoperable provider directories (i.e. the FHIR Provider Directory APIs insurers are 
required to publish under CMS-0057) also need a clear identity for the network in order 
to ensure they are searching the correct network. 
 
Need for a Standardized Network Identifier 
We recommend that a standardized network identifier be adopted to more explicitly identify 
and distinguish networks, with oversight over correct use of this identifier by insurers. Various 
segments of the identifier should be assigned and used in way that creates a consistent 
"decodable" identifier similar to the way the NHTSA VIN Decoder assembles a variety of data to 
oversee and decode VINs. 
Network identifiers can be communicated by the carriers and plan sponsors to their members, 
so that they are able to identify, beyond a doubt, which TiC file to use to look-up relevant rates 
and in many other shopping use cases. 
We have previously examined in depth the needs for such an identifier, the importance of 
convening a working group to oversee development of such an identifier, and the numerous 
use cases in which a well-defined identifier could improve data quality and empower 
consumers.  In other industries such as banking, automobile manufacturing, and retail, the 
adoption of standardized identifier schemes has made these industries dramatically more 
efficient and consumer-friendly. 
 
Need to Convene a Working Group 
To develop a robust structure and assignment process for standardized network identifier, an 
industry group should be convened to develop a standardized structure for  identifying 
networks, including â€œcustomizedâ€ versions of networks used in employer plans (see example in 
the FAQ). This group should have representation among healthcare providers, health insurers, 
and consumer advocacy groups. This standards development process should be managed in an 
open and transparent manner. Standards developed in this way can be adopted by consensus 
before rulemaking and formal standards adoption is complete. Validation that insurers are 
 
 
  
properly using standardized network identifiers should leverage existing sub-regulation update 
processes such as requiring adherence to reference schemas committed to Github as the rules 
in force at any given time. Taking a proactive approach to developing a clear identifier will 
reduce burden and confusion in the industry in production and use of TIC files. 
We have attached a proposal for the goals and structure of the working group, as well as 
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) regarding such a group. 
 
We appreciate the opportunity to provide comments and would welcome further discussion of 
anything in this submission. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Eric Ellsworth 
Director, Health Policy and Innovation 
Consumersâ€™ Checkbook/Center for the Study of Services

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Consumers' Checkbook/Center for the Study of Services; signed by Eric Ellsworth, Director, Health Policy and Innovation.
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group / Consumer organization
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Health policy and innovation role; experience analyzing Transparency in Coverage (TIC) files, provider directories, and consumer shopping use cases.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This attachment comments on a separate Transparency in Coverage proposed rule, but its concerns overlap with interoperability and transparency issues relevant to CMS-0062-P. The commenter supports network-level TIC files but urges CMS to move beyond ambiguous network names by adopting standardized network identifiers through an open, multi-stakeholder working group.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** GENERAL; API-ENDPOINT-REPORTING and FHIR-IG-REQUIRED indirectly through references to FHIR Provider Directory APIs and standardized technical artifacts.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** No CFR sections; references CMS-9882-P and CMS-0057.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR Provider Directory APIs; TIC file schemas; standardized network identifiers; NHTSA VIN decoder analogy.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Network-Level Transparency in Coverage Data**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Support
- **Rationale:** Network-level files better align data elements with contracts and price schedules, making files smaller and improving data quality.
- **Specific request:** Preserve and improve the network-level data file approach.

**Topic 2: Standardized Network Identifiers Instead of Network Names**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Network names are ambiguous, inconsistently used by carriers, and insufficient for linking plan designs, provider directories, rates, PA requirements, and medical necessity criteria.
- **Specific request:** Adopt a formal standardized network identifier with oversight over correct insurer use.

**Topic 3: Provider Directory and Interoperable API Linkage**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL
- **Position:** Clarify
- **Rationale:** Apps using FHIR Provider Directory APIs required under CMS-0057 need a clear network identity to query the correct network.
- **Specific request:** Ensure standardized identifiers can be used across TIC files, provider directories, and consumer shopping applications.

**Topic 4: Working Group and Sub-Regulatory Maintenance**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** A transparent industry working group can develop a robust identifier structure and assignment process, with schemas updated through existing sub-regulatory processes.
- **Specific request:** Convene a working group including providers, insurers, and consumer advocates; use GitHub/reference schemas to validate implementation.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

No CMS-0062-P numbered solicitation is directly answered. The comment is relevant to general RFI solicitations (S66-S82) on interoperability and transparency, and indirectly to S1-S3 because it discusses standards adoption, versioning, and sub-regulatory maintenance outside full rulemaking.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Adopt a standardized network identifier rather than relying on network names.
2. Establish oversight to ensure correct use of network identifiers by insurers.
3. Convene an open working group with providers, insurers, and consumer advocacy groups.
4. Build identifiers that support customized employer-plan network variants.
5. Validate conformance using existing sub-regulatory update processes and reference schemas.
6. Enable consumers and apps to link plans, rates, provider directories, and coverage rules accurately.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Ambiguous network names, inability to link data to plan designs and provider directories, and consumer confusion.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Degraded TIC data quality; inaccurate consumer shopping; difficulty identifying rates, networks, PA requirements, and medical necessity criteria for a specific plan.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Need for robust identifier structure, assignment processes, insurer oversight, and multi-stakeholder agreement.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** None.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Prior work by the commenter on standardized identifiers; attached FAQ and working-group proposal.
- **Examples provided:** Different names for the same network, same/similar names for different networks, provider-directory filters by plan or network, and VIN-style identifier decoding.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Consumers, employers, insurers, providers, app developers, and data users of TIC and provider directory information.
- **Economic implications:** Standard identifiers could reduce burden and confusion in producing and using TIC files and improve market efficiency.
- **Technical feasibility:** Feasible if developed through a working group and maintained through schemas/reference artifacts.
- **Patient care impact:** Indirect but meaningful for consumers choosing in-network care and understanding coverage requirements.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Supportive of transparency improvements with modifications
- **Tone:** Professional, technical, and collaborative
- **Priority level:** Medium

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "We are particularly pleased to see the proposal for introduction of network-level data files." - Context: Support for network-level TIC data.
2. "We have serious concerns around the use of a network name rather than a formal network identifier." - Context: Main objection to ambiguous network names.
3. "Apps relying on interoperable provider directories... also need a clear identity for the network." - Context: Linkage to FHIR Provider Directory APIs.
4. "Taking a proactive approach to developing a clear identifier will reduce burden and confusion." - Context: Working group and standardization recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - The comment focuses on improving transparency data quality and consumer usability.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - It proposes a structured identifier and validation through reference schemas.
- [x] **STANDARDS-MATURITY** - The commenter recommends a working group and consensus adoption before formal rulemaking is complete.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - The working group should include providers, insurers, and consumer advocates.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Accurate network identification can help consumers find in-network providers and understand coverage rules.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - The proposal is tied to TIC files, provider directories, plan designs, and consumer apps.
- [x] **VENDOR-ECOSYSTEM** - App developers using interoperable provider directories are identified as affected users.
